Chair Barragan called the special hybrid meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. in the Norwalk City
Hall, Council Chambers and via videoconference pursuant to the provisions of Assembly
Bill 361. Responding to roll call in person were Commissioner Apodaca, Commissioner
Garcia and Chair Barragan and, via Zoom, Commissioner Navas and Vice Chair Lopez.
Also present were John P. Ramirez, Director of Community Development, Gloria V.
Ramirez, Deputy City Attorney; Jill Ann Arabe, Development Services Manager, Manraj
Bhatia, Senior Planner; Andrew Arellano, Assistant Planner; and Ruth Hoffmann,
Administrative Secretary.

MEETING MINUTES

The Planning Commission approved the minutes of the Special Meeting of July 12, 2023.

PRECISE DEVELOPMENT PLAN NO. 2039
DIRECTOR APPROVAL REQUEST NO. 5
ZONE VARIANCE NO. 2022-01
Amir Houriani, Wilshire Group Funding (“Applicant”; a request to permit the construction
of a new 2,393 square foot drive-through restaurant on a 0.45-acre site. The subject
property is generally known as 12843 Norwalk Boulevard, located on the northwest
corner of Norwalk Boulevard and Adoree Street (also known as Assessor’s Parcel
Number (“APN”) 8047-005-903), in the Restricted Commercial (C-1) zone with a Public
Facilities (P-F) overlay. The project includes a request for:
(1) Precise Development Plan (PDP) No. 2039: To permit the construction of a new
  commercial building; and
(2) Director Approval Request (DAR) No. 5: To permit a drive-through establishment;
  and
(3) Zone Variance (ZV) No. 2022-01: To request deviation from drive-through
  establishment standards; and
(4) Environmental: Consider and find the project exempt from California Environmental
  Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to Section 15303 (New Construction of Small
  Structures) and Section 15332 (In-Fill Development Projects).

Chair Barragan opened the public hearing

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Senior Planner Bhatia
presented a report stating that the item before the Commission is a request to permit a
new 2,393 square foot drive-through restaurant and to deviate from drive-through
establishment standards; that the site is accessed by two driveways, one each from
Norwalk Boulevard and Adoree Street, providing clear circulation for both vehicular and
pedestrian traffic; that the project site has suffered a loss of acreage from the I-5 freeway
expansion; that the site has an access easement on the left side which is limiting the
overall developable area of the site; that the proposed development will enhance the
surrounding area by revitalizing a constrained and underutilized site, incorporate quality
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 2
Minutes of the Special Meeting  September 13, 2023

architecture, and promote economic activity; that the project, with approval of the
variance, will comply with applicable development standards of the Norwalk Municipal
Code and provide adequate vehicular circulation and pedestrian access; that, in
addition, the project is consistent with the General Plan vision of providing adequate
local-servicing commercial uses and encouraging restaurants; and that it is staff’s
recommendation that the Planning Commission adopt the resolutions attached to the
staff report subject to the Conditions of Approval contained in respective Exhibits “A”,
and consider and find the project exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) pursuant to Section 15303 (New Construction of Small Structures) and Section
15332 (In-Fill Development Projects).

Commissioner Apodaca commented on the queue length of eight (8) vehicles, and she
asked if there is a plan where additional cars can be stacked without impacting Norwalk
Boulevard should that number of vehicles be exceeded.

Senior Planner Manraj indicated that the Conditions of Approval requires the
applicant/business owner to evaluate and update their drive through operations and site
circulation if the drive-through queue were to exceed the eight (8) vehicle stacking area
or interfere with the traffic flow on Norwalk Boulevard.

Chair Barragan stated that she, too, has the same concern as expressed by
Commissioner Apodaca.

In response to Commissioner Garcia’s question how is this issue going to be addressed,
Director Ramirez stated that staff would contact the operator directly; and that should
there be an issue on Norwalk Boulevard, staff would have the ability to address this right
away, and that it would not need to be brought back to the Commission.

The applicant, Amir Houriani, stated that accompanying him this evening is his Uncle
Fred Houriani; that they have been working on this project for about six years; that they
are happy with what was presented; and that he is here to answer any questions that
the Commission may have.

In response to Commissioner Garcia’s question how many Pollo Campero
establishments do they have in and around the Los Angeles County area, Mr. Houriani
indicated that he does not have an exact number. Director Ramirez stated that the
closest one is in South Gate; and that he did a quick search and came up with at least
twenty establishments.

Since there were no other persons wishing to present testimony, Chair Barragan closed
the public hearing.

Commissioner Apodaca indicated that she already brought up the stacking of vehicles
at the drive-through; that the Adoree Street side is more available with a lot less traffic
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 3
Minutes of the Special Meeting  September 13, 2023

than Norwalk Boulevard; that the property has been vacant for many years; and other
than that, she is in support of the project.

Commissioner Garcia also commented on the irregular-shaped property being vacant
for a long time, and he stated that he is in favor of the applicant’s request.

Vice Chair Lopez concurred with the concern brought up regarding the stacking of
vehicles; and she shared that she is glad to see a development on that site which has
been vacant for quite some time.

Commissioner Navas stated that he, too, has similar concerns with the drive-through;
however, it is an irregular-shaped property.

Chair Barragan stated that she agrees with her fellow Commissioners’ comments; and
that she is glad that a developer has been found for that property.

It was moved by Commissioner Apodaca and seconded by Commissioner Garcia to:
(1) adopt Resolution No. 23-19 to approve Precise Development Plan No. 2039 subject
to the Conditions of Approval contained in Exhibit “A”; and (2) adopt Resolution No. 23-
20 to approve Director Approval Request No. 5 subject to the Conditions of Approval
contained in Exhibit “A”; and (3) adopt Resolution No. 23-21 to approve Variance No.
2022-01 subject to the Conditions of Approval contained in Exhibit “A”; and (5)
considered and found that the project is exempt from the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15303 (New Construction of
Small Structures) and Section 15332 (In-Fill Development Projects).

  Vice Chair Lopez and Chair Barragan

GENERAL PLAN AMENDMENT NO. 2022-03
ZONE CHANGE NO. 2022-05
TENTATIVE PARCEL MAP NO. 2022-04
Touraj Kavandi, NFT Real Estate LLC (“Applicant”); a request to permit the
reconfiguration of five (5) parcels into three (3) parcels to accommodate the
development of three (3) single family homes on a 0.39-acre site. The subject property
is generally known as 13310 Rosecrans Avenue, located on the southwest corner of
Rosecrans Avenue and Marilla Avenue (also known as Assessor’s Parcel Numbers
(“APNs”) 8070-023-001, 8070-023-002, 8070-023-003, 8070-023-030, 8070-023-031),
in the Restricted Commercial (C-1) zone. The project includes a request for:
(1) General Plan Amendment (GPA) No. 2022-03: To amend the General Plan Land
  Use designation from Neighborhood Commercial to Low Density Residential; and
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 4
Minutes of the Special Meeting  September 13, 2023

(2) Zone Change (ZC) No. 2022-05: To amend the Zoning Map from Restricted
  Commercial (C-1) to Single Family Residential (R-1); and
(3) Tentative Parcel Map (TPM) No. 2022-04: To reconfigure five (5) parcels into three
  (3) parcels to accommodate the development of three (3) single family homes; and
(4) Environmental: Review and recommend adoption of the associated Initial
  Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration (IS/MND) to City Council.

Chair Barragan opened the public hearing

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Senior Planner Bhatia
presented a report stating that the item before the Commission is a request to amend
the General Plan land use designation from Neighborhood Commercial to Low Density
Residential; amend the Zoning Map from Restricted Commercial (C-1) to Single Family
Residential (R-1); and to reconfigure five (5) parcels into three (3) to accommodate the
development of three (3) single-family homes at the subject site; that the three (3) single
family homes will be for sale and are proposed to be two-story construction with
approximately 2,000 square feet living space per unit and attached two-car garages.

Continuing with her presentation, Ms. Bhatia indicated that the developer hosted a
community meeting on February 28, 2023, which was attended by about eight (8)
residents, and that the feedback was positive; that there were certain comments made
that they incorporated into the conditions of approval, one of them being an 8-foot high
block wall instead of a 6-foot high wall; and that the block wall landscaping include
climbing vines and bougainvillea, trees and shrubs in the 10-foot buffer along Rosecrans
Avenue.

Ms. Bhatia shared that the proposed development will enhance the surrounding area
by revitalizing an undeveloped site, incorporate quality architecture, and add to the
City’s housing stock; that the project complies with applicable City codes, provides
adequate parking, and includes wall and landscape buffers from the commercial
corridor; that the project is compatible with surrounding uses and is consistent with the
General Plan’s goals to develop a range of well integrated housing types.

In closing with her presentation, Ms. Bhatia stated that staff is recommending that the
Commission adopt the resolutions attached to the staff report subject to the Conditions
of Approval contained in respective Exhibits “A”.

The applicant, Touraj Kavandi, NFT Real Estate LLC, stated that they have been
working on this project for about two years; and that they would ask the Commission for
their consideration approving their request.

In response to Commissioner Garcia’s question when do they anticipate construction to
start after approval of the project, Mr. Kavandi replied that as soon as they receive
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 5
Minutes of the Special Meeting  September 13, 2023

approval of the plans from the Building and Safety Department they would start
construction within six months to a year.

In response to Norwalk resident Eric Granado’s comment that the subject site includes
a Parking (P) zone, Senior Planner Bhatia shared that the P Zone is actually on
Rosecrans Avenue and not inside the property lines. Mr. Granado stated that he would
like to see his property that was rezoned many years ago, and has a house on it, go
back to residential from the P zone.

Director Ramirez indicated that at the Planning Commission meeting of September 27,
2023, they are going to bring an item for the Commission’s consideration that eliminates
the P zone from the entire City, meaning that Mr. Granado’s property will revert back to
residential probably by the end of this year after City Council consideration.

Since there were no other persons wishing to present testimony, Chair Barragan closed
the public hearing.

Commissioner Apodaca shared that she is pleased to see the development of three
houses as this will be an enhancement to the area.

Commissioner Navas stated that he was looking at the parking spaces provided and
saw four spaces for each of the homes; that the property has been vacant for a long
time, and that he is glad to see it being developed.

Chair Barragan stated that she, too, is glad to see that houses are going to be built on
the subject site; that the proposed homes are beautiful; and that she is looking forward
to seeing them come to fruition.

It was moved by Commissioner Apodaca and seconded by Chair Barragan to: (1) adopt
Resolution No. 23-22 recommending approval to City Council of General Plan
Amendment No. 2022-03; and (2) adopt Resolution No. 23-23 recommending approval
to City Council of Zone Change No. 2022-05; and (3) adopt Resolution No. 23-24
approving Tentative Parcel Map No. 2022-04 subject to the Conditions of Approval
contained in Exhibit “A”; and (5) review and recommend adoption to City Council of the
associated IS/MND.

ON ROLL CALL VOTE
AYES: Commissioner Apodaca, Commissioner Garcia, Commissioner Navas,
  Vice Chair Lopez and Chair Barragan
NOES: None
ABSENT: None

TENTATIVE PARCEL MAP NO. 2022-01
Roy Roberson, Land Strategies LLC (“Applicant”); a request to permit the subdivision
of an existing parcel of 3.86 acres into two (2) parcels. The subject property is generally
known as 11301 Firestone Boulevard, located on the northwest corner of Firestone
Boulevard and Orr and Day Road (also known as Assessor’s Parcel Number (“APN”)
8022-032-022), in the General Commercial (C-3) and Parking (P) zones. The project
includes a request for:
(1) Tentative Parcel Map No. 2022-01: To permit the subdivision of an existing parcel
  into two (2) parcels; and
(2) Environmental: Consider and find the project exempt from California Environmental
  Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to Section 15315 (Minor Land Divisions).

Chair Barragan opened the public hearing.

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Senior Planner Bhatia
presented a report stating that the item before the Commission is a request to subdivide
one parcel into two parcels; that the site is fully developed at this time with three
buildings housing Hertz Car Sales, Fast 5 Xpress car wash, and a vacant commercial
building; that this project would create an additional commercial parcel, creating higher
commercial opportunities in the City; that a Condition of Approval has been added to
the project to record a covenant to keep these two parcels under common ownership;
that if and when ownership changes, the covenant requires the building of a sewer line
on the second parcel, recordation of a reciprocal easement and recordation of a shared
parking agreement; that, as such, the project complies with the zoning code and the
General Plan; that the subdivision would not impact surrounding properties; and that
the project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA).

Further, Ms. Bhatia indicated that staff recommends that the Planning Commission: (1)
adopt Resolution No. 23-25 approving Tentative Parcel Map No. 2022-01 subject to the
Conditions of Approval contained in Exhibit “A”; and (2) consider and find the project
exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to Section
15315 (Minor Land Divisions).

In response to Commissioner Apodaca’s request for clarification of the covenant to keep
the parcels under common ownership, Ms. Bhatia stated that, yes, this is the intent of
the property owner for financing and future conveyance purposes.

Roy Roberson, Civil Engineer, Land Strategies LLC stated that he is working for the
property owner; that the buildings are already there, that no development is proposed,
that, basically, they are just drawing an imaginary line; and that, once the tentative map
is recorded, one property will become two properties.

As there were no other persons wishing to testify, Chair Barragan closed the public
hearing.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 7
Minutes of the Special Meeting  September 13, 2023

It was moved by Commissioner Garcia and seconded by Commissioner Apodaca to:
(1) adopt Resolution No. 23-25 approving Tentative Parcel Map No. 2022-01 subject to
the Conditions of Approval contained in Exhibit “A”; and (2) consider and find the project
exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to Section
15315 (Minor Land Divisions).

ON ROLL CALL VOTE
AYES: Commissioner Apodaca, Commissioner Garcia, Commissioner Navas,
  Vice Chair Lopez and Chair Barragan
NOES: None
ABSENT: None

ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OPPORTUNITIES PLAN UPDATE DISCUSSION

Director Ramirez stated that, on behalf of the City Manager Jesus Gomez, he is going
to present the City’s draft Economic Development Opportunities Plan Update. He stated
that in 2018 they initiated this plan update; that as a result of the Pandemic and the
impact to the economy, there was some movement and suggestions to perhaps
refreshing and taking another look at the City’s Economic Development Plan trying to
identify if there are any new opportunities or new constraints in order to move the City
forward in a positive direction and create employment opportunities and new revenue
streams for the City over the next generation.

Director Ramirez shared that, tonight, he is sharing a short presentation of what staff
has been doing over the last four months in terms of the City’s outreach efforts and
share with the Commission about the progress they have made over the last five years
since the original adoption of this Opportunities Plan, as well as receive feedback from
each of the Commissioners in terms of items that might be important to them as
members of the community, land use they might like to see or not see, or if there is a
particular type of service or amenities that the community would benefit from.

Continuing with his presentation, Director Ramirez introduced Sandra Lopez and
Yvonne Aguilar, who have been supporting them during this whole process and all of
their outreach efforts since May; that they have been attending Council meetings, all of
the City’s Commission meetings, including the school districts, church councils and the
Cerritos College Executive Council, and he thanked Sandra and Yvonne stating that
they have been a critical part of this process.

Director Ramirez indicated that in 2018 they identified 10 nodes and added an 11th node
towards the end of the process. He commented on each of the nodes and provided a
brief update on each one stating that, in addition, the document provides an analysis on
the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of each node. Further, Director
Ramirez stated that staff is working with property owners every week trying to nudge
them along; and that staff would like to get the Commission’s feedback, thoughts, or
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 8
Minutes of the Special Meeting  September 13, 2023

ideas that they would like to see; and that this item is going to the City Council on
October 17, 2023.

Commissioner Apodaca stated that there are a lot of upcoming exciting developments;
that they have heard comments from the public on businesses that they do not need
more of, such as laundromats, car washes, 99 cent stores, tobacco stores and check
cashing stores, and that those types of businesses could be looked at as possibly being
restrictive in the future.

Director Ramirez shared that, once the plan is adopted, they would come back to the
Commission evaluating the land uses.

In response to Commissioner Garcia’s comment that he would like to receive a copy of
staff’s presentation, Director Ramirez replied that they will provide a hard copy for
Commissioner Garcia.

Vice Chair Lopez commented on staff contacting vacant property owners; and she
asked if staff met with the property owner of the car wash located across from Tommy’s
as it appears that the car wash has been vacant for a while. Further, she also
commented on a liquor store in the same area that appears to be closed.

Director Ramirez shared that staff can reach out to them.

Commissioner Navas stated that staff has been working really hard and that it shows;
that members of the public occasionally ask the Commissioners about City projects that
are in the pipeline, and that he would ask that staff provide that information to allow the
Commissioners to share that with the residents.

Chair Barragan commented on the car wash property Vice Chair Lopez brought up.
She stated that it is located on Alondra and Pioneer; and she asked staff that the
Commission continue to be informed on upcoming developments.

Director Ramirez thanked the Commission for all of their input and with being involved
in the community, and he stated that staff is supportive of all of their efforts.

AUTHORITY

Norwalk Municipal Code (NMC) Section 17.02.210.A authorizes the Planning
Commission to review Conditional Use Permit (CUP) applications.

NMC Sections 17.04.190 and 17.11.010 require review and approval of a CUP for
childcare facility.

NMC Section 17.02.203.C.3.d.i authorizes the Director to waive a deviation of up to
twenty (20) percent from the required number of parking spaces as set forth in NMC
Section 17.03.040. The Director may refer any request to the Planning Commission for
review and determination.

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND

The 0.37-acre project site has a General Plan designation of Professional Office and
zoning of Commercial and Office (CO). The project site is located on the southeast corner
of Adoree Street and Studebaker Road (also known as Assessor’s Parcel Number
(“APN”) 8050-026-001). Surrounding the project site are single-family residential homes
to the east and west (across Studebaker Road), a vacant commercial building to the north
(across Adoree Street), and an apartment complex to the south. The subject site has
remained vacant since 2014, when it was used as a medical office. The property owner
recently completed façade renovations of the existing buildings and associated site
improvements.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

Crystal and Joy Cyprian, Joy’s Children’s Learning Center (Applicant), is requesting
approval of CUP No. 2023-03 to permit a childcare facility within an existing 2,785 square
foot single-story building and Director Approval Request (DAR) No. 2023-08 to allow an
eighteen (18) percent reduction (three spaces) from the required number of parking
spaces. The other two-story building on the site will be used for ancillary storage.

The proposed childcare facility will only operate within the single-story building. The hours
of operation are from 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. Monday through Friday with seven to eight
employees. Minor interior tenant improvements for the facility are anticipated before
operations commence.

Conditional Use Permit

The site was recently renovated with facade upgrades and improvements to enhance the
appearance and facilitate occupancy of the buildings. Pursuant to NMC Section
17.11.010 and NMC Section 17.04.190, the childcare facility requires a CUP in the CO
zone. The project complies with applicable CO development standards, except for
parking. Since no expansion of the building is proposed, the nonconforming street side
yard building setback may remain.

The proposed project is consistent with the General Plan as it provides a local-serving
commercial use for the community. The childcare facility has a curriculum specific to
infants, toddlers, and pre-schoolers, aged from zero (0) to six (6) years of age, with a
focus on social emotional development. A maximum enrollment of 20 children is also
proposed with seven (7) to eight (8) employees. The main building will include three
classrooms, kitchen area, offices, and adult and children restrooms. An outdoor play area
of approximately 1,540 square feet will be provided north of the building surrounded by
3.5 feet high of fencing. As indicated by the applicant, childcare is of high demand in the
community and the project site is a suitable location with its close proximity to surrounding
residential uses. The applicant anticipates the population served will primarily walk to the
site.

Parking and Site Circulation

The site has two existing buildings with a 14-space parking lot located between them.
Ingress and egress to the site is through an existing driveway from Studebaker Road,
located on the west side of the property. Building entrances are on the north and south
sides of the single-story building. Per the NMC, the parking requirement for the childcare
facility is one space per 200 square feet of building area and ancillary storage is one
space per 1,000 square feet, resulting in a total requirement of 17 stalls. The project is
therefore deficient by three spaces (18% of the parking requirement). Through the DAR
application, a parking reduction up to 20% may be considered provided it will not be

detrimental to public health, safety and welfare or adversely affect property values or
present and future development of the area.

Pursuant to NMC Section 17.03.060, the applicant submitted a Trip Generation and
Parking Demand study to support the request for a parking reduction. The study analyzed
trip generation for the proposed use, the square footage of the buildings, and the total
need of parking spaces per the Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip
Generation Manual. The study indicated that the proposed project would generate 31 trips
in the AM and 31 trips in the PM, with a peak parking demand of 10 parking spaces; and
it considered a staggered, scheduled drop-off and pick-up. The schedule would limit no
more than two children within 15- and 30-minute blocks for drop off and pick up and as
conditioned, families will be contractually required to arrive during those scheduled time
blocks.

The following safety mechanisms are proposed and conditioned to minimize any potential
vehicle congestion generated by the use:

-  Parents required to accompany their children into the building and sign them in and
  out
-  Limiting enrollment to a maximum of 20 children
-  Staggered drop off schedule with children arriving from 7:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. in 15
  to 30 minute increments with a maximum of two children in each block of time
-  Staggered pick up schedule between 2:30 p.m. and 6:30 p.m. in 15 minute increments
  with a maximum of two children in each block of time
-  One on-site traffic monitor will be outside and in the parking lot to control vehicles
  parking safely and leaving the site in an orderly manner
-  Two designated parking spaces for drop off and pick up
-  Security cameras strategically placed around the site

Based upon the study and with recommended conditions, the project would have
sufficient parking to accommodate the use.

Public Notification

The applicant, Joy’s Children’s Learning Center, hosted a community meeting on August
24, 2023, at the Norwalk Arts and Sports Complex. Two families with their children
attended the meeting. Positive feedback for the proposed childcare facility were shared
from the community. Public hearing notices were published in the Norwalk Patriot and
posted at locations set forth in NMC Section 1.08.030 as well as mailed to 117 property

owners and occupants within 500 feet of the property on September 14, 2023. As of the
writing of this report, staff has received no public comments.

ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT

Pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), this project will not have a
significant effect on the environment and is listed as Section 15301 Categorical
Exemption. Section 15301 exemption consists of the operation, repair, maintenance,
permitting, leasing, licensing, or minor alteration of existing public or private structures,
facilities, mechanical equipment, or topographical features, involving negligible or no
expansion of existing or former use. The proposed project involves the operation of
childcare facility within an existing 2,785 square foot building.

SUMMARY

The proposed project will enhance the surrounding area by revitalizing a vacant site and
providing a local-serving commercial use compatible with the neighborhood. The project
complies with applicable city codes, and based upon a trip generation and parking study
and recommended conditions of approval, it provides adequate parking and vehicular
circulation. It is consistent with the General Plan by providing adequate childcare services
for the needs of the community.

 INTRODUCTION

DC Engineering Group has conducted a trip generation and parking demand analysis for a
new child care facility located at 11004 Adoree Street, Norwalk, California. The analysis
was performed to assess the proposed project trip generation s effect on the surrounding
transportation circulation and the parking demand for the proposed child care facility. The
study has been prepared at the request and in compliance with guidelines and regulations
of the City of Norwalk.

This memorandum summarizes the peak parking generation and trip generation for the
proposed project. The project will require a Director Approval Request for a 20% reduction
in the required number of parking spaces per Norwalk Municipal Code (NMC) 17.03.040. As
this analysis indicates, the project trip generation is moderate and the parking supplied will
meet the peak parking demand. Additionally, the project will promote transportation
demand management (TDM) strategies to reduce the trips and parking demand even
further.

 ANALYSIS

Project Trip Generation

Trip generation estimates are based on the type of land use and the unit of measure that
relates to the appropriate trip generation factor. For example, an apartment trip rate is
usually per room, a school is per student, and a restaurant is per 1,000 square-feet.
Typically, the trip generation for three time periods is calculated. The trips are calculated for
a typical day (24 hours), the AM peak hour, and the PM peak hour. Except in rare cases,
most trip generation numbers are calculated using the Institute of Transportation Engineers
(ITE) Trip Generation Manual, 11th Edition. Using statistical data gathered in the field
across the United States for numerous land use categories, trip rate factors are derived to
be used to estimate trip generation.

The proposed project is a 2,798 square-foot child care facility with another 3,000 square-
foot building being utilized for storage. Land Use Code 565 for child care and Land Use
Code 151 for storage (mini-warehouse) from the Trip Generation Manual 11th Edition were
used to determine the project trips. The child care land use in the ITE Trip Generation
Manual has two methods for calculating trips. It can be done through the square-footage of
the land use or the number of students. Using the number of students the project will
generate 82 daily trips, 22 trips in the a.m. peak hour, and 18 p.m. peak hour trips. The
analysis used the square footage rate which determined that the proposed project trips will
be 137 daily trips with 31 trips in the a.m. peak hour and 31 trips in the p.m. peak hour.

Although the storage use was included, the small size made the trip generation negligible.

 CONCLUSION

The proposed project is to convert an existing 2,798 square-foot building into a child care
facility with three classrooms for up to 20 children and utilize another existing approximately
3,000 square-foot two-story building on site for storage. The storage building is ancillary to
the main land use being proposed, but it has been included in the calculations to provide a
conservative analysis. The existing buildings are currently vacant. There are 14 vehicle
parking spaces proposed for the child care facility. The City of Norwalk Municipal Code has
determined that the required parking for the proposed project is 17 vehicle parking spaces
(including 3 spaces for the storage). The key findings of the analysis are:

  The child care facility and storage land uses will generate a net total of 137 daily
  trips, with 31 net a.m. peak hour trips (16 inbound and 15 outbound) and 31 net p.m.
  peak hour trips (15 inbound and 16 outbound).

  The number of spaces for the proposed 2,798 square-foot child care center, per ITE,
  indicates a weekday peak parking demand of 10 spaces.

  The project will require a Director Approval Request for a 20% reduction in the
  required number of parking spaces per Norwalk Municipal Code (NMC) 17.03.040.
  As this analysis indicates, the project trip generation is moderate and the parking
  supplied will meet the peak parking demand.

  The child care facility will operate between 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m., Monday through
  Friday with 7-8 employees. The facility will operate with the following TDM
  strategies to reduce the peak hour trips and parking demand:

  Not all children will be dropped off but will access the project via walking from
  the adjacent residential neighborhoods.
  As detailed in the project description, children will arrive at the school
  between 7:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. and start times will be staggered, spreading
  out the peak demand. Two parking spaces will be designated for loading and
  unloading. Designated staff members will attend and assist with child drop off
  and pick up. Pick up times for children will also be staggered per the working
  schedules of the parents.
  Staff will be encouraged to use alternative methods of commuting to work that
  include utilizing the abundant available transit, walking, biking, and car pools.
  Information will be available to all staff about possible commuting alternatives.
